title: Threads, processes, and coordinated work
sources: CPython documentation: global interpreter lock // VERIFY implementation-specific details
masterChecklist: Threads, processes, synchronization primitives, thread safety, race conditions
Executors, queues, cancellation and safe shared-state design
whyItMatters: Waiting on files or network responses should not freeze an entire tool. At the same time, uncontrolled shared state creates bugs that appear only sometimes.
simpleExplanation: A thread is another path of work inside one process, sharing memory. A process has separate memory. Threads often suit waiting-heavy work; processes can help isolate or parallelize CPU-heavy work. A queue is a safer handoff point than many workers changing the same value.
mentalModel: Threads are coworkers sharing one whiteboard; processes are coworkers in separate rooms passing notes. A queue is an inbox that prevents everyone from grabbing the same note at once.
outcomes: Choose threads, processes, or a sequential solution deliberately.
Use a queue to communicate work.
Explain why cancellation and joining workers matter.

realWorldExample.scenario: A local report tool reads several independent files while keeping its interface responsive.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: Several workers updating one list or counter without a plan can produce timing-dependent results.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Give each worker independent input, return a result through a future or queue, set a bounded worker count, and combine results in one owner.

workedExample.code:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def label(name):
    return f'ready: {name}'

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(label, ['one', 'two', 'three']))

print(results)
explanation: ThreadPoolExecutor manages a limited set of threads.
map gives each input to label and returns results in input order.
The with block shuts the executor down after outstanding work finishes.
This example has no shared mutable state, which keeps its behavior simple.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Add a short sleep inside label and observe that output order from map still follows input order.

procedure: First ask whether sequential code is fast enough.
Classify the workload as CPU-heavy, waiting-heavy, or mixed.
Keep shared mutable state small or avoid it with returned values/queues.
Bound worker count and set timeouts at external boundaries.
Shut down or join workers and surface failures to the caller.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming more threads always make CPU work faster in CPython.
commonMistakes.why: The interpreter's execution model and overhead matter; CPU work often needs measurement or processes.
commonMistakes.avoid: Benchmark the workload and choose the simplest suitable model.

commonMistakes.mistake: Changing shared dictionaries from several workers without coordination.
commonMistakes.why: A race can make results timing-dependent.
commonMistakes.avoid: Return independent results, use a queue, or protect a clearly defined critical section.

commonMistakes.mistake: Starting workers and never collecting their exceptions.
commonMistakes.why: Failures become invisible and resources may outlive the task.
commonMistakes.avoid: Read future results and use structured shutdown.

assessment.question: What is a race condition?
assessment.answer: A result depends on unpredictable timing between operations.
assessment.explanation: Shared mutable state is a common cause.

assessment.question: Why use a bounded executor?
assessment.answer: It limits concurrent work and resource use.
assessment.explanation: Unlimited workers can make an overloaded system worse.

assessment.question: When are threads commonly useful?
assessment.answer: For many tasks that spend time waiting on I/O.
assessment.explanation: Actual choice depends on measurement and the workload.
